Title: The Paper Lantern\nCredit: Writte.text: WREN, 30s, holds a storyboard panel up to the window and squints at it.
Somebody drew this in 1974 and nobody has looked at it since.
HOLT sets down a box of film cans.
INT. ARCHIVE ROOM - PROJECTION BOOTH - LATER
A splice reel turns. The room smells of vinegar and dust.
Two frames are missing from the head of the roll.
She threads the leader by feel, the way she was taught.
Rain on corrugated steel. WREN wheels a cart of film cans out under a sodium lamp and counts them twice.
HOLT holds an umbrella over the cart and not over himself.
Forty-one. There were forty-three when we started.
Two of them went out for repair in March and nobody wrote it down.
She pulls a tarp over the cart and ties it at the corners.
The truck comes at six. Everything on that manifest has to be on the dock by then, in order, and dry.
The lamp buzzes and cuts out. Neither of them stops moving.
In the dark the cart is a long shape and the rain is louder than it was.
Bring the second cart. And the good tarp, not the one with the hole in it.
Holt goes. Wren stands in the rain with a clipboard and does not hurry.
The cart is gone. A single storyboard panel is still pinned to the window.

Title: The Proof Sheet\nCredit: Written.text: Steel shelving to the ceiling. A single bulb, swinging.
Rain on corrugated tin, loud enough to argue over.
A dual-margin scene number, the shooting-script shape: the same number printed at both margins.
ODILE sets down a box that is heavier than it looks.
Handwriting from four decades, none of it consistent.
One column, ruled in pencil, never once balanced.
Footsteps going down two at a time.
The building keeps its lights on for nobody.
Nobody is where their voice says they are.
The period-full spelling, the one the manuals print.
And the one writers actually type, missing its period.
Off camera, also missing its period.
A continued cue, carrying its extension.
Dotted abbreviations sitting inside a character name.
A hybrid: name and extension on one cue line.
The box is open now. It was not worth the trip.
A leading parenthetical, before a word is spoken.
A line, and then a beat in the middle of it.
And then the rest of it, after the beat.
Two stacked parentheticals before any dialogue at all.
They have been at this for six hours.

MORE-ANCHOR. This speech begins near the foot of the page on purpose, so that it runs over the break and has to be put back together on the other side. It keeps going well past the boundary so the rejoin has something substantial to work with, and so that the same speech doubles as the long-dialogue case the coverage table asks for, rather than spending two constructions on what is really one shape.
The label reads **DO NOT LAMINATE**, twice.
She says it *again*, and this time somebody writes it down.
The stamp is ***both bold and italic*** at once.
A styled run that **crosses the wrap boundary because it keeps** **going for long enough to need a second line**, and then stops.
This word is _underlined_ with drawn vector art.
This phrase is struck through, above the baseline.
A table rules a border below this cell, further down.
A page-wide rule crosses this whole line of text.
